site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Shabari's Patient Welcome for Rama
body: At the hermitage of the sage Matanga, the devoted ascetic Shabari had waited for years, honoring her teachers' word that Rama would one day come. The forest paths had worn beneath her patient vigil, and her heart had kept its promise through every quiet season.

When Rama and his brother Lakshmana finally arrived, she welcomed them as honored guests, offering forest fruits and cool water from her simple store. With gentle reverence, she led them through the hermitage she had tended so faithfully, her long service received with warmth and grace.

After gazing upon Rama, Shabari asked leave to rejoin her teachers in their realm, her wish fulfilled. Her lifelong devotion carried her gently to that peaceful abode, ending her wait in the bright hope she had always trusted.

stories.title: Tiny Wings, Mighty Heart
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: On the sandy shore, a little plover laid her eggs in spite of her mate's gentle warning. He feared the Ocean might roll in and sweep them away, and his worry proved true when the morning tide carried the clutch off in its foam.
The plovers would not accept such a loss. They fluttered from neighbor to neighbor until the birds gathered, and together they called upon Garuda, the great king of wings, to right the wrong.

Garuda's shadow fell across the waves, and the Ocean, trembling before such a defender, gave back the unharmed eggs. The plover family chirped together again, safe at last through persistence, friendship, and the courage to ask for help.

stories.title: The Miser Who Learned to Give
stories.source: Illisa Jataka, The Jataka, vol. II, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: In a quiet Indian village, Illisa guarded his gold so tightly he would not even buy himself a small drink of liquor. Watching his pinched and joyless life, Sakka, king of the devas, felt pity and came down wearing Illisa's very face. From the doorstep Sakka began handing out the miserly man's sacks of rice, his oxen, and his cooking pots to every passing neighbor.

When the real Illisa ran home shouting that he was the true master, the villagers only laughed and pushed him aside, certain the disguised Sakka was their kindhearted lord. At last Sakka let his heavenly light shine through, showed Illisa how light his heart had grown, and asked if he understood the joy of an open hand. Shamed and softened, Illisa fell at his feet.

From that day on the former miser poured out his wealth like water, feeding the hungry and clothing the poor. The very neighbors who had mocked him now bowed with respect, and Illisa discovered what Sakka had come to teach him: that a generous hand is the heaviest purse of all, and the heart that gives away its gold grows richer than any hidden hoard.

stories.title: The Dog Who Found Home Again
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: When famine gripped his familiar town, a dog set out in search of easier living and crossed into another country where food lay in abundance. Yet the local dogs snapped at him at every turn, and he wandered the rich streets without a single companion by his side.

He soon understood that plenty means little when there is no belonging. So the traveler turned his paws back toward his old town, where scraps were fewer but the streets were his own and welcoming barks greeted him at every corner. He settled again among his friends.

Gathered with the dogs who knew him, he shared what he had learned: a modest life among familiar friends is worth far more than a foreign feast earned in fear. With their warm welcome around him, he ended his days contentedly at home.

stories.title: The Mouse-Maid Finds Home
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: In a quiet forest hermitage, a kindly sage pulled a trembling baby mouse from the claws of a crow. With a whispered mantra he shaped her into a human girl, and he and his wife raised her with tender care as their own beloved daughter, teaching her the gentle ways of the world.

When she was grown, the hermit searched for the strongest husband he could find, asking the Sun, the Cloud, the Wind, and the Mountain in turn. Each answered that another was more powerful than itself, until the Mountain at last pointed to mice, who bore patiently through stone.

The girl smiled when she saw a mouse nearby, feeling a sudden, natural warmth toward him. The hermit blessed her and changed her back into a mouse, and she happily chose her small bridegroom. Her parents rejoiced, for their daughter had at last returned to her true and loving home.
